postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:64 — [P1][confidence 100][advisory/simplification] `if href.present? && href.start_with?('/')` leaves ordinary relative links such as `images/a.png` resolving under Discourse's `/embed/` route and rewrites protocol-relative `//cdn.example/a.png` onto the article host; using URI resolution for a shared `a[href], img[src]` path removes both duplicated branches and preserves every valid relative-reference form despite the counter-argument that most feeds use root-relative URLs.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real bug in the absolutize_urls method. Looking at lines 56-72 of app/models/topic_embed.rb, the code only handles URLs that start_with?('/'), meaning: 1) Ordinary relative links like 'images/a.png' (no leading slash) won't be converted and will resolve incorrectly under Discourse's /embed/ route. 2) Protocol-relative URLs like '//cdn.example/a.png' do start with '/' so they'll be incorrectly rewritten to 'http://host//cdn.example/a.png'. These are real edge cases that the current implementation doesn't handle correctly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:59 — [P1][confidence 100] `prefix << ":#{uri.port}" if uri.port != 80 && uri.port != 443` drops an explicit port whenever it equals the other scheme's default, so `https://example.com:80/article` rewrites embedded links to `https://example.com/...` and fetches a different endpoint.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a logic flaw in the absolutize_urls method at line 59. The code `prefix << ":#{uri.port}" if uri.port != 80 && uri.port != 443` only appends the port if it's neither 80 nor 443. However, this doesn't account for scheme mismatches - for example, if the URL is `https://example.com:80/article`, the port 80 is non-standard for HTTPS but would be dropped because the condition excludes port 80 regardless of scheme. Similarly, `http://example.com:443/path` would drop port 443. This could cause relative URLs to be rewritten incorrectly, pointing to different endpoints than intended.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:4 — [P2][confidence 100][advisory/wrong-shape] `t.integer :topic_id, null: false` stores a topic identity already derivable from the adjacent `post_id` without any invariant tying the two, so a row whose post belongs to another topic makes `topic_id_for_embed` open one discussion while updates revise another; the current creator writing matching values does not protect later writers, and deleting `topic_id` makes the illegal state and one field-to-maintain unnecessary.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that storing both topic_id and post_id creates a data integrity risk. However, looking at the diff, the TopicEmbed model is created with both fields for valid reasons: topic_id enables efficient lookups via topic_id_for_embed() without joining through posts, and the code in import() always creates them together atomically within a transaction. The 'derivable' relationship is intentional denormalization for query efficiency. The claim about 'later writers' causing inconsistency is speculative - the diff shows only one code path that creates TopicEmbed records, and it correctly sets both values. This is a design opinion about normalization, not a verifiable bug in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:41 — [P2][confidence 100][advisory/coupling] `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` couples one missing-page retrieval to a synchronous scan and import of every feed item, so a single iframe request performs unrelated topic updates and grows linearly with the entire feed despite the reuse benefit of calling existing polling code.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a design concern in the diff. Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb lines 38-42, when a topic embed is not found, the code calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` synchronously. Looking at app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb, the `poll_feed` method iterates through ALL RSS items (`rss.items.each`) and calls `TopicEmbed.import` for each one. This means a single iframe request for one missing embed URL triggers a full synchronous scan of the entire feed, which is a legitimate architectural/performance concern. This is not a bug per se (the code works), but it's a valid scope/architecture concern about coupling and performance that a reasonable reviewer would flag.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:15 — [P2][confidence 75] `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` keys identity on the unnormalized presentation of a URL, so default-port, host-case, and fragment variants of the same article bypass the unique index and create separate Discourse topics.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first uses the raw URL string for lookup, and the database has a unique index on embed_url. URLs like 'http://example.com:80/path' vs 'http://example.com/path', or 'http://Example.com/path' vs 'http://example.com/path', or URLs with fragments would be treated as different URLs despite pointing to the same resource. This could lead to duplicate topics being created for the same article. The diff shows no URL normalization is performed before storage or lookup in the import method at line 15.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:15 — [P2][confidence 100] `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` performs a check-then-create outside the transaction, so concurrent imports both fetch and create the same topic before one `TopicEmbed.create!` loses the unique-index race and aborts with `RecordNotUnique`.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a race condition. Looking at the diff in app/models/topic_embed.rb, line 15 shows `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` which is outside the `Topic.transaction do` block that starts at line 19. The transaction only wraps the creation logic (lines 19-27), but the check for existing embed happens before the transaction. If two concurrent requests both check and find no existing embed, they'll both enter the transaction and try to create a TopicEmbed with the same embed_url. Since there's a unique index on embed_url (shown in the migration at line 12: `add_index :topic_embeds, :embed_url, unique: true`), one will fail with RecordNotUnique. This is a valid race condition bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3 — [P1, confidence 100] `create_table :top_topics, force: true do |t|` drops the already-shipped `top_topics` table and all ranking data whenever this edited migration is re-run, causing irreversible data loss before recreating an empty table.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that adding 'force: true' to the migration will cause data loss when the migration is 're-run'. However, Rails migrations are designed to run only once - they are tracked in the schema_migrations table and won't be re-run in normal operation. The 'force: true' option is commonly used in migrations to handle cases where the table might exist from a failed previous migration attempt. This is not a bug that would cause data loss in production since migrations don't get re-executed. The diff shows this is a new migration file being created, and the change from the original (without force: true) to the new version (with force: true) is a reasonable defensive coding practice for migrations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:27 — [P1, confidence 100] `$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` commits the deduplication key before retrieval succeeds, so a fetch failure makes every subsequent queued retry silently return success without doing work for 60 seconds and leaves the embed displaying Loading.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a race condition issue in lib/topic_retriever.rb. Looking at the code: `retrieved_recently?` sets the Redis key with `$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` and expires it for 60 seconds BEFORE `perform_retrieve` is called. If `perform_retrieve` (which calls `fetch_http` -> `TopicEmbed.import_remote`) fails for any reason, the key remains set for 60 seconds, causing all subsequent retrieval attempts to return early from `retrieved_recently?` returning true. This means the embed will show 'Loading' for up to 60 seconds even though no successful retrieval occurred. The key should ideally be set after successful retrieval, not before.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:50 — [P1, confidence 100] `return if user.blank?` silently drops every embed retrieval when the configured import username is missing or stale, while the controller keeps returning a successful Loading page that reloads forever with no actionable error for the site owner or visitor.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue. In lib/topic_retriever.rb:50, `return if user.blank?` silently exits when the embed_by_username setting doesn't match a valid user. Looking at the flow: embed_controller.rb calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic) and renders 'loading' which (per loading.html.erb) reloads the page every 30 seconds. If the username is misconfigured, fetch_http returns early, no TopicEmbed is created, and the loading page keeps reloading indefinitely with no error feedback. This is a legitimate UX/correctness bug where misconfiguration leads to an infinite loading loop.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:37 — [P1, confidence 75] `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)` records the new content hash without checking whether `revisor.revise!` persisted the preceding post update, so a callback-aborted save is reported as an imported revision and all future polls skip the content permanently; although validations are intentionally bypassed, Rails callbacks still return false from `save` and the hash update survives independently.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue in the diff. Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 30-37, when content has changed, `revisor.revise!` is called but its return value is not checked. Then `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)` is called unconditionally. If the revise operation fails for any reason (callbacks returning false, etc.), the content_sha1 is still updated, which means future polls will see the hash matches and skip the content permanently, even though the actual post content was never updated. This is a legitimate bug where the hash update should be conditional on the revision succeeding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — [P1, confidence 100] `doc = Readability::Document.new(open(url).read,` follows attacker-controlled redirects after the one-time hostname check, so a permitted embedding page can redirect the server into an internal HTTP service and publish the extracted response as a forum topic.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real SSRF vulnerability. In topic_embed.rb:48, `import_remote` uses `open(url).read` which follows HTTP redirects. While `topic_retriever.rb` checks that the URL's host matches `embeddable_host` before calling `fetch_http`, this check only validates the initial URL. If the permitted external page returns an HTTP redirect to an internal service (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/), Ruby's `open` will follow it, fetch internal content, and the Readability parser will extract and publish that content as a forum topic. This is a classic SSRF via open redirect bypass.
